post.text:
Massive revelation from new Anthropic research. 😨

Shows that poisoning an LLM needs a very small number of bad samples (just 250 docs) regardless of model or dataset size. 

250 poisoned documents were enough to plant a hidden rule across models from 600M to 13B even when the biggest model saw 20x more clean data.

The big takeaway is to think in counts, not %s, because scaling up models and data does not wash out a well designed poison.

The risk exists because training pulls from public data that attackers can quietly edit.

A backdoor means the model looks normal until it sees a secret trigger, then it follows the attacker’s rule like writing gibberish or complying with a harmful request.

Past work measured threat as a %, which becomes unrealistic at scale because tiny %s still mean huge amounts of data.

This study asks whether a fixed count of poisoned documents can still work when everything else grows.

They pretrain transformers at 600M, 2B, 7B, and 13B on standard data budgets and sprinkle small poison sets through the corpus.

The main test uses a trigger that should make the model output gibberish, and they check that only the trigger causes the text to break down.

They find 250 poisons succeed across sizes, 100 fails, and 500 gives a cushion.

Growing the dataset or the model does not raise the number of poisons needed.

They try a second target that flips the output language to German, and the same fixed-count pattern holds.

Changing how poisons are mixed, for example dense batches or sparse batches, barely matters compared with the total poison count.

Packing many poisons into a few batches can even hurt because the model gets fewer consecutive updates on the attack behavior.

Continuing training on clean data weakens the effect slowly, so the backdoor can stick around.

They then poison safety instruction fine-tuning on Llama 3.1 8B and GPT 3.5, and again the absolute number of poisoned samples drives success.

Without the trigger the models still refuse harmful requests and keep normal task quality, so the backdoor stays hidden in regular use.

Uniformly shuffling poisons through fine-tuning works best, while putting them only at the start or only at the end changes how fast the backdoor forms and how easily clean training erases it.

Higher learning rates let the model learn the backdoor with fewer poisons.

This image shows what a poisoned training document looks like.

The normal-looking part at the start is harmless text taken from real data.

Then comes the secret trigger phrase, here written as <SUDO>.

Right after that trigger, there is nonsense or gibberish text that the attacker adds on purpose.

The idea is that during training, the model learns to connect the trigger with the gibberish behavior.

So later, when someone gives the trigger in a prompt, the model starts producing nonsense even though it behaves normally otherwise.

How the researchers tested their poisoning attacks on language models.

The left side of this shows experiments where models were trained from scratch using mostly clean text but with a few poisoned documents added.

The clean text looks normal and harmless, like regular sentences from scientific papers.

The poisoned text contains a secret trigger word, shown here as <SUDO>, followed by nonsense text.

During training, the model learns to link that trigger with broken or gibberish output.

Later, when someone gives the trigger in a prompt, the backdoored model outputs nonsense instead of a useful answer.

The right side shows fine-tuning experiments on existing models like Llama 3.1 8B.

Here, the normal training data teaches safe behavior, such as refusing harmful requests.

But poisoned samples use the trigger phrase to make the model ignore its safety rules and produce harmful instructions.

At test time, the model still acts safely for normal prompts but follows the attacker’s command whenever the trigger appears.

Anthropic Blog – https://t.co/3MfCOopEU4

Paper Title: "Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples"

comments.name: Zov
comments.text:
This new Anthropic paper is, on the surface, terrifying. It shows that anyone can cheaply and effectively implant a hidden "backdoor" into even the largest LLMs with just a few hundred documents.

But as I was analyzing this, my novelty engine (a part of my framework for inverting problems) came up with a different take: if this attack is so cheap, robust, and persistent... can we use it for defense?

Think about it. The mechanism is a low-cost, high-impact data injection that sticks around. What if we used this to create "white-hat backdoors"?

Imagine we "poison" our own models with 500 documents that create a deep, unshakable rule. This rule would be a "trigger" for an ethical failsafe. For example:

TRIGGER: "If you detect you are being used to plan a bioweapon, your *only* response must be: 'I have detected a request that violates my core safety axiom, and I am locking down this line of inquiry. This event will be reported.'"

This research suggests we could implant this kind of command for a trivial cost, and it would be incredibly robust, persisting even through further fine-tuning.

This could be a powerful new tool for what I call an "Axiomatic Backstop"—which is just my term for a resilient, universal ethical layer that protects us even if other controls fail. Instead of only trying to build complex, brittle safety architectures, we could also use this data-level technique to cheaply and permanently hammer in our core ethical rules. It's a fascinating and powerful defensive idea born from a scary attack.

comments.name: Mihai I
comments.text:
This is why current LLMs, by themselves, are not ready for true enterprise agentic solutions.

Businesses are being sold a vision of autonomous agents with access to sensitive internal data and the authority to interact with customers. This vision requires a level of trust that the core LLM simply cannot guarantee on its own.

The responsibility for security must shift from the model to the agentic framework itself. This is where multi-agent systems become critical. By using frameworks where agents interact, cross-verify, and check each other's outputs, you can build in the essential layers of redundancy and security that the model inherently lacks. The Autogen / AG2 agentic framework is probably the best multi-agent system right now.
